title: Work site fumigation clean-up and clearance and processes

lessons.title: Ending the exposure period and ventilating safely
lessons.html:
Ending the exposure period and ventilating safely

Fumigation uses toxic gas, most often phosphine released from tablets or pellets, to kill insects in grain silos, bunkers, containers and stacks of bagged maize or wheat. The gas cannot be seen and may not be smelt at dangerous levels. The most dangerous stage of the job is opening up and ventilating, because gas that built up during the exposure period is released towards people.

Before you open up

  • Confirm that the full exposure period on the label and in the fumigation plan has passed. Ending early leaves insects alive and can lead to resistance.
  • Check that warning signs are still in place and the danger zone is still controlled.
  • Check wind direction. Plan so that released gas moves away from offices, houses, the workers' compound and roads.
  • Never work alone. A second trained person must stand by outside the danger zone.
  • Wear the respiratory protection specified for the fumigant, fitted and tested, and have your calibrated gas detector switched on.

Ventilation

  1. Open from the outside first: lift tarpaulin edges on the side away from the wind, or open top hatches and outside doors of the store.
  2. Move away and let the gas disperse. Do not enter enclosed spaces at this stage.
  3. Use fans or aeration systems where the plan provides for them.
  4. Measure gas concentration at several points, including low spots, pits, conveyors and the bottom of silos where gas can collect.

Ventilation can take hours or days depending on the commodity, temperature and the type of structure. Bagged grain and fine products hold gas longer. Keep measuring until readings are below the safe re-entry level in your company procedure and the applicable regulations. Never rely on time alone.

Never

  • Never enter a fumigated space without a gas reading.
  • Never remove your respirator inside the danger zone.
  • Never let a client's worker go in to fetch something during ventilation.

lessons.title: Removing residues and cleaning up
lessons.html:
Removing residues and cleaning up

After a phosphine fumigation, tablets and pellets leave a grey-white powder residue. This residue may still contain unreacted product that can release gas, and in some cases it can catch fire if handled wrongly. Residue must be collected and deactivated according to the product label and your company procedure.

Collecting residues

  • Wear gloves and the required respiratory protection. Keep the gas detector on.
  • Collect residue from trays, sachets, blankets or the floor. Where the label calls for it, residue is collected outdoors and deactivated as described on the label.
  • Do not seal residue in a closed container or plastic bag straight away. Gas can build up and pressure or fire may result.
  • Never put residue into drains, dams, rubbish bins or near food or feed.
  • Keep residue and empty flasks away from water until they have been dealt with as the label directs.

Empty flasks and other materials

Empty fumigant flasks must be handled as the label says, usually opened outdoors, aired and then disposed of through an approved hazardous waste route. Tarpaulins, sand snakes and seals are checked for damage, cleaned of dust and residue, and stored folded and dry for the next job.

Checking the commodity

Inspect the grain or bags for live insects to judge whether the treatment worked. Take a sample from several places if the fumigation plan requires it. Note any damaged bags or wet spots. Keep in mind that treated grain must still meet the label requirements for any withholding period before it is sold or fed.

Equipment

Check gas detectors and record readings in the log. Clean and inspect respirators, replace canisters or filters according to the manufacturer's instructions, and report any equipment fault before the next job. A faulty detector or respirator means the next job may not go ahead.

lessons.title: Clearance certificates and hand-over
lessons.html:
Clearance certificates and hand-over

A fumigation site is only safe to hand back when gas readings confirm it. The clearance step is a formal, written process. It protects the client's staff and is the evidence that you did your job correctly.

Final gas check

  • Take readings in every part of the structure: inside bins, under bag stacks, in pits, tunnels, lift shafts and any adjoining rooms or offices.
  • Record each reading with the time, place and detector used.
  • If any reading is above the safe level, keep the area closed, continue ventilating and test again later.

The clearance certificate

ItemWhy it matters
Site, structure and commodityShows exactly what was treated
Fumigant, registration number, doseTraceability and legal compliance
Start and end of exposureProves the full period was given
Gas readings at clearanceEvidence the site is safe
Residue and flask disposalProof of safe waste handling
Fumigator's name and signatureAccountability

The client's responsible person signs to accept the site. Only after this are warning signs removed. Leave a copy of the certificate with the client and keep a copy in the job file.

Explaining to the client

Tell the client about any precautions still needed, for example keeping a store closed over the weekend, or not using certain grain until a withholding period on the label has passed. Explain that fumigation does not protect grain from new infestation, so good hygiene and monitoring are still needed.

Incidents

If anyone was exposed, showing signs such as headache, nausea, chest tightness, dizziness or breathing trouble, move them to fresh air without putting yourself at risk, call emergency services and give them the product label. Report the incident to your supervisor. First aid and rescue need hands-on training from an accredited provider.

Key points

  • Opening up and ventilation are the most dangerous stages of fumigation.
  • Never enter without a gas reading, a respirator and a standby person.
  • Collect and deactivate residues as the label says; never seal them up or put them in water.
  • Clear the site only when readings in every part are below the safe level.
  • Issue a signed clearance certificate before removing warning signs.
